findings.headline: Goldthorpe Towns Fund programme only 2% deployed: £4.3m allocation had just £97k outturn
findings.detail: Goldthorpe Towns Fund - DLUHC shows planned expenditure of £4,302,481 but actual outturn of only £97,276, representing an underspend of £4,205,205 (98%).
findings.matters: Towns Fund is external government regeneration financing with specific deployment requirements and clawback provisions; a 98% underspend indicates delivery failure on externally-funded strategic programme and may affect future funding tranches
findings.quote: Goldthorpe Towns Fund - DLUHC 4,302,481 97,276 -4,205,205

findings.paper_title: 6b. End of Year Capital Programme Performance 2025 26 Covering Report
findings.headline: HRA deferred reroofing and central heating work to prioritise emergency repairs
findings.detail: Within the Housing Revenue Account capital programme, the council deferred scheduled reroofing and central heating schemes to ensure emergency works were completed. This maintenance deferral resulted in £1.3M slipping into 2026/27. Supplementary works on component replacements, major adaptations and major voids continue, with remaining committed work at £1.1M.
findings.matters: Deferral of planned maintenance work (reroofing and central heating) to accommodate emergency repairs signals a maintenance backlog in HRA housing stock that will require significant future capital investment and may indicate asset condition pressures.
findings.figures: £1.3M reroofing and central heating deferred; £1.1M component/adaptation work remaining
findings.quote: However, the decision to postpone rooﬁng schedule and central heating schemes to ensure emergency works were delivered has led to a total of £1.3M slipped into 26/27.

findings.paper_title: 6b. End of Year Capital Programme Performance 2025 26 Covering Report
findings.headline: Health on High Street partnership project (£3.4M) delayed by NHS lease agreement hold-ups
findings.detail: Health on the High Street is a partnership project with NHS and local health providers to establish a health and wellbeing hub in Barnsley town centre. Slippage of £3.362M reflects delays in the council's contribution to NHS outpatient works capital costs and, critically, delays to lease agreement finalisation that have been deferred into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Partnership projects with NHS experiencing lease agreement delays demonstrate coordination risk in major regeneration schemes and may indicate broader challenges in aligning third-party partners on delivery timelines.
findings.figures: £3.362M slippage
findings.quote: The majority of the slippage reflects the reproﬁling of the Council's contribution to the capital costs of NHS outpatient works and the agreement for the lease being delayed into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 6b. End of Year Capital Programme Performance 2025 26 Covering Report
findings.headline: Goldthorpe Towns Fund (£4.2M) slipped by prolonged grant funding agreement negotiations and developer changes
findings.detail: The £23.1M Goldthorpe Towns Fund, government-funded through the Town Deal initiative, has £4.205M slipping into 2026/27. The Goldthorpe Commercial Investment Fund project faces delays from "prolonged negotiations concerning grant funding agreements, planning and legal dependencies, as well as changes in developer arrangements," with contractual commitment and defrayal delayed into the next financial year.
findings.matters: Government-funded regeneration projects experiencing delays in grant agreement negotiations signal grant funding risk and coordination challenges that could impact future delivery timelines and create borrowing or revenue funding pressure.
findings.figures: £4.205M slippage from £23.1M programme
findings.quote: This delay is primarily attributable to prolonged negotiations concerning grant funding agreements, planning and legal dependencies, as well as changes in developer arrangements. As a result, contractual commitment and defrayal of funding has been delayed into the 26/27 financial year.

findings.paper_title: 6b. End of Year Capital Programme Performance 2025 26 Covering Report
findings.headline: £29.1M capital programme slippage (23% of budget) driven by external factors and complexity
findings.detail: The council achieved £94.6M capital spend against an approved £124.7M budget, with £29.1M slippage accounting for most of the shortfall. The report states this variance is "primarily a result of scheme slippage across the programme" where "expenditure plans are expected to be utilised in a future year rather than the current year, due to events largely outside of the Council's control." Growth & Sustainability directorate accounts for £23.2M of the slippage, with detailed explanations provided for multiple major schemes.
findings.matters: A 23% slippage rate on a £124.7M capital programme indicates material delivery challenges and execution risk that would concern lenders assessing the council's capacity to deliver planned infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: £29.1M slippage out of £124.7M programme; £23.2M in Growth & Sustainability directorate
findings.quote: This variance is primarily a result of scheme slippage across the programme, with the majority relating to schemes delivered by the Growth & Sustainability Directorate.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate fell 0.33% below target, partly due to new support scheme raising household bills
findings.detail: Council Tax collection reached 96.17% against a stretch target of 96.5%, a shortfall of 0.33%. The council attributes this to introducing a new Council Tax Support scheme in April 2025 that required some households to pay more, combined with cost-of-living pressures on those not eligible for support. Business Rates collection also fell 0.06% short of a 98% target at 97.94%.
findings.matters: Collection rate decline, even if small, signals rising household difficulty paying council bills. A trend of further decline would reduce the council's income certainty and ability to service debt. The council's own policy change (raising charges) may also mask worsening underlying collection pressure.
findings.figures: Council Tax 96.17% actual vs 96.5% target (shortfall 0.33%); Business Rates 97.94% vs 98% (shortfall 0.06%)
findings.quote: Council Tax collection reached 96.17% by the end of 25/26, slightly lower than the stretch target of 96.5%. This small shortfall is mainly due to the introduction of a new Council Tax Support scheme in April, which required some households to pay more, coupled with the continuing rise in the cost of living affecting those not eligible for support.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care pressures of £2.7M driven by demand and complexity in residential and nursing placements
findings.detail: Older People services overspent by £1.4M (mainly £0.8M in locality team staffing due to agency reliance, plus £0.4M in placement costs), and Working Age Adults by £1.3M (mainly £1.2M in purchasing, related to residential/nursing/supported living placements, plus £0.3M in specialist team staffing for overtime and agency). The council notes increased demand and complexity, with cost increases not offset by client and health contributions.
findings.matters: Like children's services, adult social care shows unplanned demand escalation in expensive placement-based services. The council is managing this through agency staffing (expensive short-term fix) rather than sustainable capacity planning, signalling the service is reactive and under-resourced.
findings.figures: Older People overspend £1.4M, Working Age Adults £1.3M; staffing/agency pressures £0.8M + £0.3M
findings.quote: Pressures have also been experienced within Older People and Working Aged Adult Social Care Services of £2.7M. This is due to an increase in demand and the complexity of care needs.

findings.headline: Only 76% of £12.6M approved savings delivered in 2025/26; LAC placement savings missed entirely
findings.detail: The council approved £12.6M of efficiency savings in the 25/26 budget but delivered only £9.6M. Children's Services achieved just 38% delivery (£1.4M of £3.9M), with the critical £1.9M LAC placement savings missing entirely because internal foster care recruitment failed and in-borough provision slipped. Growth & Sustainability missed £1.0M (£2.6M of £3.6M) due to delays in asset management strategy and street lighting dimming.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings in the year they are committed signals weak operational control and unreliable financial forecasting. The LAC savings miss is particularly concerning: it shows the council planned to do something operationally (recruit foster carers, build in-borough capacity) but did not execute, forcing it to absorb the cost from reserves instead.
findings.figures: £9.6M delivered of £12.6M target (76%); Children's £1.4M of £3.9M (38%); LAC placements £0M of £1.9M
findings.quote: A total of £12.6M of recurrent efficiency proposals were agreed as part of the 25/26 budget. Of these £9.6M have been delivered in full. The agreed efficiency savings of £1.9M on Looked After Children's placements have not yet been delivered. These efficiencies were to be delivered as part of the Children in Care Sufficiency Strategy, and although work continues to deliver against this target, due to lower than anticipated recruitment of in-house foster carers combined with slippage in delivery of the Council's in-borough provision, which is not expected to be operational until June 2026, these savings were not delivered.

findings.headline: Minimum £23M funding gap forecast over MTFS to 2028/29 with savings plan not yet detailed
findings.detail: The February 2026 MTFS update identified a minimum £23M funding gap across the three-year planning period. To address this, the council agreed a 4-point savings strategy but only high-level direction is stated: contain social care demand, improve efficiency council-wide, review LGA benchmarking outliers, and review policy choices. The detailed delivery plan is not expected until summer 2026, leaving significant implementation risk.
findings.matters: An unspecified £23M savings requirement over three years signals structural imbalance in the council's finances. The absence of a detailed plan by the reporting date suggests either the savings do not yet exist or the council is hoping reserve drawdowns can bridge the gap longer-term, both poor signs for repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £23M minimum funding gap 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: the estimated cost pressures over planning period continue to outstrip the available funding, meaning a minimum funding gap of £23M is currently forecast. To address this gap Members have agreed a 4-point savings plan, with the Council's Senior Management Team being tasked with bringing forward detailed proposals for Member consideration and approval during 26/27.

findings.headline: £19.3M High Needs/SEND cumulative deficit increased by £5.4M in-year
findings.detail: The council's cumulative High Needs deficit grew from £13.9M carried forward to £19.3M by year-end. The in-year deficit of £8.1M was driven by increased Education Health and Care Plan numbers and costs (£1.2M), more children placed in expensive independent non-maintained special schools (£2.9M), and £2.3M for alternative provision tutoring. While government is consulting on funding 90% of this (£3.7M), the deficit remains subject to statutory override only until 2027/28, after which the council must fund it.
findings.matters: This is a structural deficit growing faster than planned, with partial government support ending in less than two years. The council faces a known liability it cannot fully offset, representing a significant future budget pressure that will impact financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £19.3M; in-year increase £5.4M; government funding proposal covers £3.7M
findings.quote: Note the current High Needs (SEND) deficit of £19.3M, an increase of £5.4M in 2025/26. This deficit is currently subject to a statutory override by Government to 2027/28.

findings.headline: Children's looked-after placements £8.5M overspend driven by 80 more external placements than planned
findings.detail: The council budgeted for 372 looked-after children but had 410 by year-end (38 more). More critically, it planned 65 external residential/IFA placements but ended with 145 (80 more than planned). These external placements are significantly more expensive; 21 children cost over £8,000/week, averaging £12,090/week. The council's recruitment of in-house foster carers has failed to materialise and in-borough provision slipped to June 2026.
findings.matters: Unplanned demand escalation in the most expensive social care service, with no effective containment strategy, signals demographic or social pressures the council cannot manage. This is driving the single largest budget overspend and reflects a failure to deliver planned placement efficiencies.
findings.figures: LAC 410 actual vs 372 planned; external placements 145 actual vs 65 planned; high-cost placements 21 at £12,090/week average; cost pressure £8.5M
findings.quote: At the start of 25/26 the Council planned for a closing position of 372 LAC (across all placement types); however, as of 31 March 2026 the number of LAC totalled 410 (38 more than planned). Furthermore, the planned profile mix anticipated a total of 65 external residential and IFA placements (10 and 55 respectively), with the expectation that most placements would be family based (i.e. in-house foster or connected carers), which carry a lower cost. However, the number of external residential and IFA placements at 31 March was 145 (60 residential + 85 IFA placements), 80 more than planned.

findings.headline: £13.1M general fund overspend funded by reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council overspent its approved budget by £13.1M in 2025/26, which is being funded by drawing down earmarked reserves set aside for this purpose. This is an improvement of £1.3M on the Q3 position but still represents a significant unplanned deficit. The council's strategic reserves have moved from £224.3M to £206.6M, a total reduction of £17.7M when including other reserve movements and earmarkings.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to cover operating deficits signals the council is spending above sustainable levels and eating into its financial buffers; lenders view reserve drawdowns for current spending as a warning sign of structural budget problems.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £224.282M, closing £206.556M; overspend £13.1M
findings.quote: It is proposed that the remaining £13.1M of cost pressures are funded via a drawdown of the Budget Mitigation Reserve specifically earmarked for this purpose and in line with the overall MTFS.

findings.headline: Council is deferring £27M of fixed-rate borrowing indefinitely while under-borrowed by £254M, betting on interest rates falling
findings.detail: Despite a 70% fixed-rate borrowing target, the council is not undertaking new long-term borrowing while rates remain elevated. Meeting the target would require £27M of additional loans over the period to 27/28 at an estimated cost of £1.5M per year in additional interest. Instead, the council is using internal borrowing—temporarily drawing on cash reserves and earmarked balances—and has an under-borrowed position of £254.2M as at 31 March 2026. This strategy will reverse when rates fall.
findings.matters: This strategy defers costs but creates refinancing risk if cash reserves deplete before rate forecasts materialise. Lenders assess whether reserves are sufficient to sustain this under-borrowed position or whether the council will be forced to borrow at unfavourable rates if cash runs out.
findings.figures: £27M borrowing deferred, £1.5M annual interest cost deferred, £254.2M under-borrowed position, £63M underlying borrowing need over 27/28
findings.quote: If the Council were to continue to meet the 70% fixed rate borrowing target, this would require in the region of £27M of debt to be secured in additional fixed rate loans over the period to 27/28. Based on current long-term borrowing rates this would cost the Authority approximately £1.5M in additional interest payments per year.

findings.headline: MRP policy changes from annuity to straight-line method, more than doubling the annual debt repayment charge from 26/27
findings.detail: The council's Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) — the mandatory annual charge to reduce the capital financing requirement — is switching methodology in 26/27. This increases the annual charge from £5.345M in 25/26 to £13.658M in 26/27 (excluding PFI schemes), or £19.306M when including PFI arrangements. This represents a material increase in the amount the council must set aside each year to repay debt.
findings.matters: A sudden doubling of mandatory annual debt repayment directly reduces revenue budget flexibility and cash flow available for services. Lenders assess whether a council can absorb this charge without depleting reserves or impairing service delivery.
findings.figures: £5.345M (25/26 actual) rising to £13.658M (26/27 planned), or £19.306M with PFI
findings.quote: the approved MRP Policy for 26/27 has changed from charging on an annuity basis to a straight line method and thus the £5.345M 25/26 MRP charge (excluding PFI schemes) shown in the table below will rise to £13.658M in 26/27 (excluding PFI's), (£19.306M including PFI's)

findings.headline: Waste and recycling service escalated to high risk with major safety and quality failures requiring service redesign
findings.detail: The Safety and Quality Programme for domestic waste and recycling has been escalated back to Senior Management Team as a high-risk actual issue. The service is undergoing major change involving all aspects, with continued work needed to improve overall safety and quality. Planned round redesigns are due to begin in summer 2026 and governance arrangements are being adjusted to reflect ongoing risks and service status.
findings.matters: Service quality and safety failures at high-risk level require significant investment to remedy and may impact council's cost base or reputation.
findings.figures: No specific figures; high response rating; redesigns planned for summer 2026
findings.quote: Major change programme involving all aspects of the service. Continued work to improve overall safety and quality required. Governance arrangements dynamic to reflect ongoing risks and service status. Planned round redesigns to begin in Summer 26.

findings.headline: ICB resources shrinking by at least 50% directly impacting council's safeguarding services and Care Act compliance
findings.detail: Due to national reorganisation of Integrated Care Boards (ICBs), resources in South Yorkshire and Barnsley ICB will shrink by at least 50%. This directly impacts council safeguarding services and other Care Act duties through ICB vacancy freezes and staff at-risk restructuring. While the ICB has business continuity plans for core services, there will no longer be capacity for other areas. The consultation was reopened in March 2026 with new governance scheduled to begin 1st July 2026.
findings.matters: External partner capacity loss directly constrains the council's ability to discharge statutory safeguarding duties and meet Care Act requirements, potentially creating compliance risk.
findings.figures: ICB resources shrinking by at least 50%; new governance begins 1st July 2026
findings.quote: Due to the organisational change required of ICB's nationally, the ICB resources in South Yorkshire and Barnsley will shrink by at least 50%. This is directly impacting on the safeguarding services and other duties required under the Care Act in terms of a vacancy freeze and many staff now being at risk due to the re-organisation.

findings.headline: Adult social care capacity to plan future demand has deteriorated to red status due to staff shortages
findings.detail: Meeting statutory responsibilities under the Care Act 2014 is classified as an actual (not potential) risk. The council's capacity to ensure future needs and demands are factored into the Medium-Term Financial Strategy has deteriorated: the status was explicitly moved to red because capacity to deliver this work is limited due to staff shortages. This comes amid high demand into the service driven by pandemic legacy (loss of independence), cost of living crisis impacts, and volatility in the care market.
findings.matters: Inability to forecast future demand impacts financial planning accuracy and increases risk of unfunded cost pressures emerging mid-year.
findings.figures: No specific figures; status downgraded to red in this review
findings.quote: Capacity to deliver this work limited due to staff shortages. Status moved to red.

findings.headline: SEND costs escalated from medium to high risk with exponential demand growth; government covers only 80% of accumulated deficit
findings.detail: SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) has been re-graded from medium to high risk. Pressures for places and funding are increasing exponentially. The council submitted a SEND Reform Plan in June 2026, which if approved by DfE will allow access to funding equivalent to 80% of the council's cumulative SEND deficit to 31st March 2026. However, the remainder stays as a pressure on the council, and government intentions regarding deficits during 2026 to 2028 are unknown.
findings.matters: Escalation to high risk indicates senior leadership's assessment that demand and cost pressures in SEND cannot be absorbed without material financial impact. Partial government funding creates ongoing unfunded liability.
findings.figures: 80% of cumulative SEND deficit to 31st March 2026 covered; remainder unresolved
findings.quote: Pressures for places & funding for children with Special Educational Needs & Disabilities {SEND] continue to increase exponentially. Government are currently consulting of reforms in this area with the council set to submit its SEND Reform Plan on the 18th June 26. Subject to approval, this will allow the Council to access equivalent of 80% of its cumulative SEND deficit to 31st March 26, with the remainder being a pressure for the Council.

findings.headline: Council's 2025/26 budget will overspend by £14M with £68M+ cost increase forecast to 2028/29
findings.detail: The council is facing a £14M overspend in the current year. Over the three-year period to 2028/29, costs are forecast to increase by at least £68M. Against this, the council faces a budget gap of at least £23M to 2028/29, despite having already delivered over £150M in efficiency savings since 2010. A four-point saving plan has been approved but is still in development, with detailed proposals to be presented to elected members in late spring/early summer.
findings.matters: This is an actual (not potential) financial sustainability crisis that directly threatens the council's ability to fund services without further savings or borrowing.
findings.figures: £14M overspend 2025/26; £68M+ cost increase through 2028/29; £23M budget gap to 2028/29; £150M+ efficiencies already delivered since 2010
findings.quote: The cost of delivering council services during 2025/26 is set to exceed agreed budgets by £14M with the estimated cost over the period through to 2028/29 set to increase by a minimum of £68M.

findings.headline: S151 officer conditions all future capital borrowing on successful delivery of unwritten savings plan
findings.detail: The S151 officer explicitly conditions new capital borrowing 'on the basis that the budget recommendation relating to the preparation of a detailed savings / financial sustainability plan is satisfactorily concluded.' The plan does not yet exist (due summer 2026). Given the council's significant existing debt from prior policy decisions and the £30M structural deficit, the officer is signalling that new borrowing for capital projects cannot proceed until the council proves it can reduce operating costs.
findings.matters: The CFO is flagging that new debt would be imprudent without first solving the revenue budget crisis. This is a governance constraint on capital projects and signals debt sustainability concerns.
findings.figures: New borrowing costs forecast £2.1M (26/27), £3.1M (27/28), £7.1M (28/29); council holds 'significant levels of debt' from prior capital investment
findings.quote: Furthermore, I have been clear in my advice that the a dditional borrowing factored into the MTFS to fund future capital priorities [aforementioned increase in the Capital Financing Requirement] should only proceed on the basis that the budget recommendation relati ng to the preparation of a detailed savings / financial sustainability plan is satisfactorily concluded.

findings.headline: £51M reserves depleted over four years; further £6.8M draw proposed in 26/27 leaving reserves near minimum thresholds
findings.detail: The council has drawn £51M from reserves in the past four fiscal years (22/23–25/26 projected). The 26/27 budget proposes a further £6.8M draw. This compounds the council's inability to balance ongoing operations. The S151 officer notes the original reserves were built during the 2010–2020 austerity period through 'successful efficiency and other savings programmes', but those are now exhausted. A £15M 'budget resilience reserve' is to be held back, but this is described as a contingency for 'extremis' scenarios only.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite, non-renewable buffer. Depleting them without structural revenue corrections is unsustainable and leaves the council with no shock absorption.
findings.figures: £51M reserves drawn past 4 years; £6.8M proposed 26/27 draw; £15M resilience reserve retained; £20M Minimum Working Balance held
findings.quote: The Council has had to use substantial [£51M] reserves to support the budget in the past four fiscal years [22/23, 23/24, 24/25 & 26/26* projected]. This has only been possible because the Council accumulated significant reserves following a sustained period of successful efficiency and other savings programmes, particularly in the decade following the commencement of austerity in 2010 [to 2020].

findings.headline: Children's Social Care costs rising exponentially; £12M pressure in 25/26 with £18M forecast over planning period
findings.detail: Looked After Children placement numbers have stabilised but the cost per placement is rising sharply. The 25/26 outturn shows £12M pressure despite this stabilisation. The MTFS forecasts £10M additional cost in 26/27, then £4M in each of 27/28 and 28/29. The service is exploring mitigation but 'it is unlikely that these will deliver material savings in the short/medium term', indicating the council expects costs to remain elevated.
findings.matters: CSC is demand-led and cost-driven by placement types (residential, independent foster) outside council control. Exponential per-placement cost growth is not manageable through volume reductions.
findings.figures: £12M pressure 25/26; £10M 26/27; £4M each in 27/28 and 28/29; total £18M over planning period
findings.quote: Whilst the numbers of Looked After Children have stabilised (reflecting the additional investment / work within Children's Services) the cost of provision particularly within residential and independent foster care placements continues to rise exponentially (current £10M pressure reported for 25/26). Whilst the service continues to explore options to mitigate these pressures, it is unlikely that these will deliver material savings in the short/medium term.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficits of £15M (27/28) and £27M (28/29) forecast, totalling circa £30M p.a., with no funding solution identified
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts recurring deficits starting 27/28: £15.087M in 27/28 and £27.264M in 28/29. The S151 officer states that 'Assuming no change in existing service levels, there will be significant deficits in the budget every year from 27/28 onwards, that together will total circa. £30M per annum by the end of this planning cycle.' The officer concludes 'without significant immediate and ongoing corrective action it will not be possible to maintain current service levels over the medium term.' The government's announced 0.5% cut from 28/29 suggests deficits will persist.
findings.matters: Annual deficits of £27M+ cannot be bridged from reserves indefinitely. This signals mandatory service reductions, further tax rises, or financial failure.
findings.figures: £15.087M gap 27/28; £27.264M gap 28/29; ~£30M p.a. by end of planning cycle; 0.5% government cut from 28/29
findings.quote: Assuming no change in existing service levels, there will be significant deficits in the budget every year from 27/28 onwards, that together will total circa. £30M per annum by the end of this planning cycle. Furthermore, if the next Spending Review and Funding Settlement in 29/30 do not see a significant increase in funding, which currently looks unlikely given that the 2025 Autumn Budget announced a 0.5% cut in the Local Government  Departmental Expenditure Limit from 28/29, then annual deficits will become the norm thereafter.

findings.headline: No savings delivery in 2026/27; budget bridged by £6.8M reserves with major delivery plan due summer 2026
findings.detail: The council proposes zero savings for 26/27, instead balancing from one-off reserves 'purely based on this being a temporary bridging strategy'. The S151 officer notes evidence of recent savings non-delivery or delays 'due to increasing complexity'. The Chief Executive must submit detailed savings plans by summer 2026 for 27/28 implementation, but these have not yet been developed. This is a one-year pause masking a structural inability to find and deliver permanent solutions.
findings.matters: Reserve bridging without a credible savings plan is unsustainable. The pattern of non-delivery and delays is a red flag that the planned savings from 27/28 onwards may not materialise.
findings.figures: £6.8M reserve draw in 26/27; £150M cumulative savings since austerity began 2010; £12.1M delivered in 25/26
findings.quote: Considerable savings have been required to balance budgets since the onset of austerity in 2010 through to the current budget in 25/26  [£150M p.a. in total, of which £12.1M relates to 25/26]. It is becoming more difficult to both identify and deliver sa vings with recent ev idence of non-delivery or severe delay s due to increasing complexity. Given this, there are no savings proposed for 26/27, with the budget instead being balanced from one off reserves, purely based on this being a temporary bridging strategy to allow more time to work up the detailed savings plans that will be required from 27/28 onwards.

findings.headline: Equal Pay employment tribunal claims received August 2025; liability unquantified and outcome pending
findings.detail: The council received formal employment tribunal claims on 27 August 2025, responded 18 September 2025, and is analysing validity while awaiting the preliminary hearing date. The S151 officer states 'it is yet to be confirmed whether the Council has a present obligation arising from past events', meaning the liability is unquantified and contingent. This creates balance sheet and financial sustainability uncertainty.
findings.matters: Employment tribunal awards can be material and sudden. Until the hearing and outcome, the council cannot quantify the exposure or plan for it.
findings.figures: None; liability amount unknown pending tribunal
findings.quote: The Council received notice of Equal Pay claims against it from the Employment Tribunal on 27 August 2025. The Council responded to these claims on 18 September 2025 and is currently analysing their validity and awaiting the date of the Employment Tribunal preliminary hearing. As such, it is yet to be confirmed whether the Council has a present obligation arising from past events.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care funding gap from 4.1% National Living Wage increase and rising complexity in caseloads
findings.detail: The National Living Wage rising 4.1% to £12.71 will drive significant ASC provider fee increases. These exceed the available funding from the settlement and the 2% ASC council tax precept, requiring the council's base budget to make up the shortfall. Additionally, the council is experiencing cost pressures from an increase in both the number and complexity of younger adult and older people caseloads 'for the first time in several years'. The S151 officer explicitly requires Cabinet and SMT scrutiny of commissioning arrangements.
findings.matters: ASC is demand-led and driven by National Living Wage changes outside council control. Rising complexity signals case numbers or acuity are growing, not stabilising.
findings.figures: 4.1% NLW increase to £12.71; £2.5M additional ASC pressures in 25/26; £4.6M forecast ASC provider fees cost in 26/27
findings.quote: The impact of the increase in the National Living Wage for 2 6/27 will place significant upward pressure on fee levels for next year and beyond . These additional costs will exceed the available funding provided through the revised funding settlement and the proposed 2% increase in the Adult Social Care council tax precept, with the Council's own base budget and savings elsewhere required to make up the shortfall.

findings.headline: Savills review identified unresolved governance and financial transparency issues between the council and its housing ALMO that require action planning.
findings.detail: While Savills confirmed the HRA is 'financially well managed,' the review found governance 'opportunities to improve' between the council and Berneslai Homes. The report called for 'greater transparency around the management fee' and recommended strengthening the ALMO Board's role and the council's client function. An action plan is 'currently being pulled together' with no completion date specified.
findings.matters: Unresolved governance issues between landlord and ALMO increase risk of cost overruns or delivery failures; lenders assess local authority control of delegated entities; this is an open issue requiring sustained management.
findings.figures: Berneslai Homes management fee £17.3M for 26/27
findings.quote: The report states greater transparency is needed around the management fee and, this has progressed during the 26/27 business planning cycle. Also to note the report states that there are opportunities to improve, whilst acknowledging the effective partnership working.

findings.headline: The government's target for Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) C rating by 2030 would require a £42M five-year programme the council cannot currently afford.
findings.detail: Central government has set a 2030 deadline for all social housing to reach EPC C. Meeting this would cost £42M over five years. The council has explicitly excluded this from the business plan, noting 'there are currently too many unknowns and it is not currently affordable or deliverable within the plan.' The council's stock includes homes nearly 100 years old, driving high maintenance costs.
findings.matters: A regulatory target deadline may force unplanned spending or regulatory action; aging stock drives higher maintenance and leaves less headroom for growth investment.
findings.figures: £42M estimated for EPC C programme over 5 years; stock includes homes nearly 100 years old
findings.quote: The Government and Council's net zero ambitions have not been factored into the business plan as there are currently too many unknowns and it is not currently affordable or deliverable within the plan.

findings.headline: Treasury review increased HRA debt charges by £2M; interest payable is forecast to grow from £2.1M to £2.5M across the business plan.
findings.detail: A treasury management review of HRA cash flows resulted in a £2M upward revision of debt charges to the account. Interest payable is forecast to increase from £2.092M in 26/27 to £2.503M by 2030/31. The council plans £30M of borrowing across 2026–31 to fund capital programmes.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce operational headroom; debt sustainability depends on rental income stability and the regulatory environment not deteriorating further.
findings.figures: £2M increase in debt charges; interest payable £2.092M rising to £2.503M; £30M planned borrowing 2026–31
findings.quote: The Council's treasury management team reviewed the HRA's cash flow in line with the Council's Financial Regulations. As a result, the debt charges to the HRA have been increased by £2M.

findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance costs are under pressure; Savills review found financial control issues at the council's ALMO including unexplained variances in repair costs.
findings.detail: The council faces 'an increasing order book in relation to repairs and maintenance works and increasing disrepair claims.' Savills' independent review noted issues in Berneslai Homes' financial controls, specifically 'movements in repairs totals between forecasts and outturns' at year-end 2024/25. An action plan has been committed but the issues indicate cost volatility risk.
findings.matters: Repair cost overruns are a documented risk; ALMO control weaknesses increase exposure to unforeseen spending; disrepair claims represent financial and legal liability.
findings.figures: Repairs budget £26.4M for 26/27; control issues identified in 24/25 year-end reporting
findings.quote: The report notes issues around Berneslai Homes financial controls particularly in relation to the 24/25-year end and movements in repairs totals between forecasts and outturns.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law (damp and mould) compliance will require unquantified additional spending when phases roll out October 2026 and October 2027.
findings.detail: Phase 1 commenced October 2025 with £1M budgeted for Building Safety Compliance in 26/27. Subsequent phases are planned for October 2026 and 2027 but 'will be quantified during 2026'. This creates exposure to unplanned costs in a business plan already under pressure.
findings.matters: Unquantified future compliance costs could emerge; regulatory failure carries legal risk and reputational damage; this adds to pressures behind the identified capital savings gap.
findings.figures: £1M allocated for phase 1 Building Safety Compliance in 26/27; phases October 2026 and 2027 costs unknown
findings.quote: Further phases will be rolled out in October 2026 and 2027 which may require additional resources. These will be quantified during 2026.

findings.headline: Rents are set at the CPI+1% policy ceiling (4.8%), while 56% of tenants are on Universal Credit and bad debt provision is doubling.
findings.detail: The 4.8% increase is required to balance 26/27 and is at the policy limit. Government may introduce rent convergence (allowing additional £1–2/week increases) but will not announce details until after this budget is finalised, leaving years 2–5 planning uncertain. Meanwhile, Universal Credit covers 56% of tenants; bad debt provision is forecast to grow from £0.44M to £0.48M, indicating rising collection pressure.
findings.matters: Lenders assess debt sustainability against reliable rental income; policy uncertainty undermines forward projections; UC-driven collection risk erodes net income available for debt servicing.
findings.figures: 4.8% increase = £4.48/week average; bad debt provision £0.44M (2025/26) rising to £0.48M (2030/31); 56% of tenants on UC
findings.quote: For the Council to be able to set a balanced HRA budget for 26/27 and allow for a continuation in existing levels of work and priority investments in relation to decency and compliance a 4.8% rent increase is required.

findings.headline: The council must identify £18M in capital programme savings or slippage across years 2-5 (£4.5M p.a.) to maintain a balanced 30-year business plan.
findings.detail: A structural affordability gap means all future capital programmes—including new build acquisitions and energy efficiency investments—are marked as indicative and subject to review. The council explicitly states these £18M in cuts are required regardless of rent convergence policy. This constrains housing growth and the EPC C programme.
findings.matters: Major investment commitments (new homes, energy efficiency) are at risk of deferral or cancellation; the council cannot fund existing stock maintenance and growth simultaneously.
findings.quote: Cabinet should note that future savings or reprioritisation of £4.5M p.a. for years 2-5 totalling £18M is required to balance the plan. All programmes included are indicative and subject to review in the next business planning cycle.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 Treasury and Prudential Indicators Q2
findings.headline: PFI costs are driving General Fund financing costs above forecast
findings.detail: The ratio of General Fund financing costs to net revenue stream is 15.37% actual vs 14.44% estimated. However, non-PFI financing costs (7.28%) are lower than forecast (7.48%), indicating the overall increase is entirely attributable to higher than expected PFI payments.
findings.matters: Higher than forecast PFI costs reduce available revenue for services and suggest either committed PFI obligations exceeding plan or unit costs rising faster than anticipated, constraining the council's fiscal flexibility
findings.figures: GF ratio 15.37% vs 14.44% estimate; GF excl. PFI 7.28% vs 7.48% estimate
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream GF 14.44% 15.37%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 Treasury and Prudential Indicators Q2
findings.headline: Capital expenditure is only 26% of annual plan at mid-year
findings.detail: Q2 actual capital expenditure totals £39.557M against an annual estimate of £154.320M. General Fund is £28.563M of £122.273M (23% of plan), and Housing Revenue Account is £10.994M of £32.047M (34% of plan). At half-way through the financial year, the council has delivered only a quarter of planned capital investment.
findings.matters: Capital spending significantly below forecast suggests delivery delays or implementation constraints that could affect the council's ability to complete planned improvements and may require revised financing
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure Total 154.320 39.557

findings.paper_title: Barnsley MBC - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - AG Committee 12 Nov 2025
findings.headline: Pension fund valuation identified as significant risk with high estimation uncertainty
findings.detail: Pension fund net balance valuation is flagged as a significant risk due to high estimation uncertainty in defined benefit pension liability valuations. This applies to both the council and Berneslai Homes (subsidiary). No specific findings reported yet but auditors note this remains outstanding work.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are often the largest long-term obligation; valuation errors directly impact financial position and may signal underfunding of future benefit obligations.
findings.figures: Not yet specified in completed work
findings.quote: The BHL net pension fund liability is considered a significant risk at group level due to the significant estimation uncertainty of defined benefit pension liability valuation.

findings.paper_title: Barnsley MBC - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - AG Committee 12 Nov 2025
findings.headline: Significant land and buildings valuation risk identified covering £1.17 billion of assets
findings.detail: The council revalues land and buildings on a rolling five-yearly basis. Auditors identified this as a significant risk due to the size (£1.17bn) and sensitivity to assumptions in depreciated replacement cost calculations, particularly for specialised assets like schools and leisure centres. Auditors engaged their own valuation expert to challenge the council's valuations.
findings.matters: Large property valuations are inherently subjective; if assets are overstated, this distorts the council's asset base and borrowing capacity. The need for auditor expert challenge indicates complexity and estimation risk.
findings.figures: Land and buildings portfolio £1.17 billion based on 2024-25 draft accounts
findings.quote: This valuation represents a significant estimate by management in the financial statements due to the size of the numbers involved (some £1.17 billion for land & buildings and council dwellings based on 2024-35 draft accounts) and the sensitivity of this estimate to changes in key assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Barnsley MBC - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - AG Committee 12 Nov 2025
findings.headline: Materiality threshold increased to 2% of gross expenditure (from 1.5%) based on improved control assessment
findings.detail: The auditors raised their materiality benchmark from 1.5% to 2% of gross expenditure to £14.98m, citing the council's stable financial reporting team, good track record of quality financial statements, and low numbers/sizes of prior-year errors. This reflects auditor confidence in the control environment rather than deterioration.
findings.matters: A higher materiality threshold can mean smaller errors go unreported; while this reflects auditor confidence, it suggests less scrutiny of smaller misstatements.
findings.figures: Materiality £14.98m at 2% of gross expenditure (prior year 1.5%); Performance materiality £11.24m
findings.quote: The benchmark percentage has increased from 1.5% in the prior year in recognition of our understanding and risk assessment as identified above and to reflect developments in materiality levels across the sector.

findings.paper_title: Barnsley MBC - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - AG Committee 12 Nov 2025
findings.headline: Multiple audit adjustments to consolidation accounts including £972k omitted pension asset
findings.detail: Auditors identified five material adjustments in the group accounts: a £972k pension asset omitted for the parent company, £20,293k actuarial gain omitted from Berneslai Homes pension liability, incorrect prior-year disclosure of £471k vs £422k for BHL pension reserve, and missing PPE disclosures. Management agreed to correct all.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities and assets are key indicators of long-term financial commitments and risks; material omissions and errors suggest control weaknesses in pension accounting consolidation.
findings.figures: £972k pension asset omitted; £20,293k actuarial gain omitted; BHL pension reserve incorrectly disclosed £471k instead of £422k
findings.quote: Pension Asset - £972k relating to the parent company (BMBC) was omitted. ... The group accounts did not include disclosures on Property Plant and Equipment (PPE). Considering this is a significantly material balance, a PPE note was added to group accounts for this year and prior year.

findings.paper_title: Barnsley MBC - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - AG Committee 12 Nov 2025
findings.headline: IFRS 16 Leases implementation led to material right-of-use asset misstatement requiring correction
findings.detail: The council's first application of the new IFRS 16 standard (effective 1 April 2024) resulted in right-of-use vehicles, plant and equipment being overstated by £3.06m (recorded as £8,729k instead of £5,668k). This adjustment was identified during audit and management corrected it. IFRS 16 requires recognition of right-of-use assets and liabilities on the balance sheet where previously these were off-balance-sheet operating leases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the true lease liabilities and asset valuations, and the initial implementation error shows the control environment for new standards required tightening.
findings.figures: Right of Use Assets overstated by £3,061k (£8,729k vs £5,668k corrected figure)
findings.quote: Right of Use Assets - Right of Use Vehicles, Plant, Furniture & Equipment was incorrectly stated as £8,729k where it should have been £5,668k.

findings.headline: Overall revenue overspend of £4.2m in 2024/25, with additional £3.8m cost pressures emerging in Q1 2025/26
findings.detail: Despite a balanced budget set for 2025/26, the Council identified £3.8m of cost pressures by the end of Q1. This follows a £4.2m net overspend in 2024/25 (1.6% of budget), though substantially down from £18.1m in 2023/24. The Council delivered 95% of its £8.4m savings target in 2024/25 and faces a £12.6m savings requirement for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Emerging pressures in new financial year despite balanced budget indicate underlying demand/cost issues are not fully resolved; £12.6m savings target is ambitious given track record and tightening financial space.
findings.figures: Net overspend 2024/25: £4.2m (1.6% of £256.6m budget); Q1 2025/26 cost pressures: £3.8m; 2025/26 savings target: £12.6m; 2024/25 savings delivery: 95% of £8.4m target
findings.quote: At the end of quarter 1 2025/26 the Council identified an overall £3.8m cost pressure on its revenue budgets.

findings.headline: High external borrowing at £566m (8% of revenue) with refinancing risk if interest rates remain elevated
findings.detail: Barnsley has a relatively high level of external borrowing compared to other Metropolitan authorities, reflecting its town centre and regeneration strategy. Financing costs represent 8.04% of net revenue stream in 2024/25. While the Council has no long-term variable rate borrowing, internal borrowing is subject to interest rate risk. Debt maturity profiles are designed to minimise refinancing risk but this remains a vulnerability in a high-rate environment.
findings.matters: High debt service costs constrain financial flexibility; refinancing risk means higher-than-expected rates could force further budget cuts or reserve draws; limits capacity to address other pressures.
findings.figures: Gross external borrowing £566m in 2024/25; financing costs 8.04% of net revenue stream; forecast borrowing stable at £561m (2025/26), £553m (2026/27), £546m (2027/28) with financing costs 7.48%-8.31%
findings.quote: Gross external borrowing (without accrued interest) (£m)" shows "2024/25 566" and "Financing costs as a percentage of net revenue stream" shows "2024/25 8.04%

findings.headline: Council has depleted £34m of reserves over three years and is using them unsustainably to balance budgets
findings.detail: Between 2022/23 and 2024/25, the Council drew down £34m from reserves, primarily driven by overspends in children's social care. The £4.2m 2024/25 overspend was covered by drawing from a Budget Resilience Reserve (reduced from £23m to £18m in-year). The Council's own strategy acknowledges this use of reserves 'should not be used in this way, except as a temporary measure.'
findings.matters: Continued reserve depletion to cover structural overspends is unsustainable and reduces financial resilience for unforeseen events. Current minimum working balance of 7% (£20m) may be inadequate if reserves continue to be drawn.
findings.figures: £34m drawn from reserves over 2022/23 to 2024/25; Budget Resilience Reserve reduced from £23m to £18m during 2024/25; minimum working balance equivalent to 7% of 2025/26 net General Fund budget (£20.0m)
findings.quote: the Council has used £34m of its own reserves over the period 2022/23 to 2024/25 (driven partly by the overspends in children's social care

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit now projected at £16.6m by March 2027, not eliminated as Safety Valve agreement expected
findings.detail: The Council's Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education was meant to eliminate the DSG deficit by 2026/27 through £22.9m of additional payments. The cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2025 was £13.9m (including an in-year deficit of £3.5m), and revised forecasts show it will reach £16.6m by end March 2027. This puts the Council at risk of not meeting its Safety Valve agreement obligations and losing conditional future funding.
findings.matters: Failure to meet Safety Valve terms could result in loss of conditional DfE funding and has reputational impact. The deficit will eventually fall on the General Fund when the statutory override ends in March 2028 if not resolved.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £13.9m as at 31 March 2025 (comprising £12.2m carried forward from 2023/24 plus £3.5m in-year deficit, offset by £1.7m Safety Valve payment); revised projected cumulative deficit of £16.6m by end March 2026/27
findings.quote: The outturn in June 2025 indicated that the final closing cumulative DSG deficit balance as of 31 March 2025 was £13.9m, comprising a £12.2m deficit carried forward from 2023/24, but also an in-year deficit of £3.5m

findings.headline: Children's services overspend of £6.8m, down from £17.4m but still substantial and driving reserve depletion
findings.detail: The overspend fell significantly year-on-year but remains a major pressure on the Council's finances. The Council has developed a Financial Sustainability Plan with senior leadership engagement and is showing early signs that cost increases are beginning to level out, though the auditor retained an improvement recommendation. Unit costs remain high due to complexity of needs in specific cohorts including adolescents.
findings.matters: Persistent high-cost pressures in statutory children's services limit financial flexibility and force use of reserves to balance budgets, which the Council acknowledges is unsustainable.
findings.figures: £6.8m overspend in 2024/25 (13% of £53m net budget); compared to £17.4m in 2023/24 (45% of £38.8m); budget growth forecast at only 4% for 2025/26 (£55.3m)
findings.quote: The overspend was driven principally by ongoing cost pressures were in children's services (£6.8m), also a reduction from an overspend of £17.4m in 2023/24.

findings.headline: Financing costs are consuming a larger share of General Fund revenue than budgeted
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is 15.37% in Q1 actual compared to the 14.44% estimate, showing debt servicing is running above forecast. Even excluding PFI, the ratio is 7.28% actual against 7.48% estimate.
findings.matters: Higher-than-budgeted debt service leaves less revenue available for service delivery and signals affordability may be tighter than planned, which is material to lenders assessing the council's ability to service debt
findings.figures: 15.37% actual vs 14.44% estimate; excluding PFI 7.28% actual vs 7.48% estimate
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream GF 14.44% 15.37%

findings.headline: Capital expenditure is running at only 10% of annual budget in Q1 for both General Fund and HRA
findings.detail: General Fund capital spending reached £11.822m of £118.008m budgeted; HRA reached £2.656m of £29.608m; total capital £14.478m of £147.616m estimate. This substantial underspend suggests project delays or slower-than-planned delivery across the council's capital programme.
findings.matters: Large capital underspends raise questions about project delivery capability and whether the council can execute its planned investment schemes, which directly concerns lenders assessing management quality and financial stability
findings.figures: General Fund £11.822m of £118.008m; HRA £2.656m of £29.608m; Total £14.478m of £147.616m
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure General Fund 118.008 11.822

news_drafts.lead: Towns Fund is external government regeneration financing with specific deployment requirements and clawback provisions; a 98% underspend indicates delivery failure on externally-funded strategic programme and may affect future funding tranches

news_drafts.headline: HRA deferred reroofing and central heating work to prioritise emergency repairs
news_drafts.lead: Deferral of planned maintenance work (reroofing and central heating) to accommodate emergency repairs signals a maintenance backlog in HRA housing stock that will require significant future capital investment and may indicate asset condition pressures.
